sections.heading: V-D Probabilistic Security Analysis
sections.text: Let p i p_{i} denote the probability that an attack successfully bypasses layer i i . Under the assumption of layer independence (each layer uses different detection mechanisms and failure modes), the probability of an attack successfully penetrating all n n layers is: P s ​ u ​ c ​ c ​ e ​ s ​ s = ∏ i = 1 n p i P_{success}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}p_{i} (3) For a multi-turn crescendo attack facing Layers 3, 4, 5, and 7, with estimated individual bypass probabilities based on the literature: • p 3 p_{3} (Semantic Firewall): 0.30 (semantic paraphrasing can evade intent classification) • p 4 p_{4} (State Machine): 0.15 (cumulative state tracking is hard to evade) • p 5 p_{5} (Anomaly Detection): 0.20 (novel patterns may evade signature matching) • p 7 p_{7} (Human Escalation): 0.05 (human reviewers catch most flagged cases) P s ​ u ​ c ​ c ​ e ​ s ​ s = 0.30 × 0.15 × 0.20 × 0.05 = 0.00045 = 0.045 % P_{success}=0.30\times 0.15\times 0.20\times 0.05=0.00045=0.045\% (4) Under the idealized independence assumption, this represents a significant reduction from > > 90% ASR (single-layer defense). However, the independence assumption must be critically examined. Sensitivity Analysis Under Correlated Failures : In practice, layers sharing semantic understanding (L3, L4, L5) exhibit correlated failure modes—an attack that evades semantic intent classification may also evade trajectory analysis and anomaly detection. We model this using a heuristic interpolation (common in reliability engineering [ 27 ] ) with a correlation factor ρ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \rho\in[0,1] where ρ = 0 \rho=0 represents full independence and ρ = 1 \rho=1 represents complete correlation: P c ​ o ​ r ​ r ​ e ​ l ​ a ​ t ​ e ​ d = P i ​ n ​ d ​ e ​ p ​ e ​ n ​ d ​ e ​ n ​ t ( 1 − ρ ) × P w ​ o ​ r ​ s ​ t ​ _ ​ l ​ a ​ y ​ e ​ r ρ P_{correlated}=P_{independent}^{(1-\rho)}\times P_{worst\_layer}^{\rho} (5) V-D 1 Cross-Domain Defense Composition We introduce a formal framework for quantifying the diversity benefit of cross-domain defense composition—addressing the open question raised by Littlewood and Strigini [ 63 ] regarding whether diversity in redundant systems provides meaningful security benefit against systematic attacks. Definition (Feature Overlap). Each defense layer D i D_{i} operates on a feature representation ϕ i ​ ( x ) \phi_{i}(x) of the input x x . The feature overlap between two defenses is: ω ⁡ ( D i , D j ) = M ​ I ​ ( ϕ i ​ ( X ) , ϕ j ​ ( X ) ) min ⁡ ( H ⁡ ( ϕ i ​ ( X ) ) , H ⁡ ( ϕ j ​ ( X ) ) ) \omega(D_{i},D_{j})=\frac{MI(\phi_{i}(X);\phi_{j}(X))}{\min(H(\phi_{i}(X)),H(\phi_{j}(X)))} (6) where M ​ I MI denotes mutual information and H H denotes Shannon entropy. ω ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \omega\in[0,1] measures the degree to which two defenses “see the same thing” in the input—i.e., the extent to which their detection mechanisms share information. Observation (Domain Distance Reduces Overlap). Defenses originating from different fields operate on fundamentally different feature types: Layer 2 (perimeter) uses syntactic token patterns; Layer 3 (semantic firewall) uses embedding-space representations; Layer 4 (state machine) uses temporal state trajectories; Layer 5 (anomaly detection) uses statistical distributional features; Layer 6 (consensus) uses cross-model agreement signals. Cross-domain pairs inherently have lower ω \omega than same-domain pairs because their feature extraction mechanisms share minimal computational structure. Proposition 3 (Diversity-Correlation Bound). For defenses D i D_{i} , D j D_{j} with feature overlap ω ⁡ ( D i , D j ) \omega(D_{i},D_{j}) , the failure correlation satisfies: ρ ⁡ ( f ​ a ​ i ​ l i , f ​ a ​ i ​ l j ) ≤ ω ⁡ ( D i , D j ) + ϵ \rho(fail_{i},fail_{j})\leq\omega(D_{i},D_{j})+\epsilon (7) where ϵ \epsilon accounts for shared vulnerability to attacks that are agnostic to feature type (e.g., attacks that succeed regardless of detection mechanism). Following the beta-factor model from reliability engineering (IEC 61508), we bound ϵ ≤ β C ​ C ​ F ⋅ min ⁡ ( p i , p j ) \epsilon\leq\beta_{CCF}\cdot\min(p_{i},p_{j}) where β C ​ C ​ F \beta_{CCF} is the common cause failure fraction. For CivicShield’s cross-domain layers, β C ​ C ​ F ≤ 0.15 \beta_{CCF}\leq 0.15 based on the fraction of the attack taxonomy (Table IV ) that is feature-agnostic. When ω \omega is small (cross-domain defenses using different feature types), failure correlation is bounded to be small. The full derivation, including the tightened ϵ \epsilon characterization, is given in Appendix A . Corollary (Composition with Bounded Correlation). For n n defenses with pairwise feature overlaps { ω i ​ j } \{\omega_{ij}\} , the combined bypass probability satisfies: ∏ i p i ≤ P c ​ o ​ m ​ b ​ i ​ n ​ e ​ d ≤ ∏ i p i ⋅ exp ⁡ ( ∑ i < j ω i ​ j ⋅ h ⁡ ( p i , p j ) ) \prod_{i}p_{i}\leq P_{combined}\leq\prod_{i}p_{i}\cdot\exp\bigg(\sum_{i<j}\omega_{ij}\cdot h(p_{i},p_{j})\bigg) (8) where h ⁡ ( p i , p j ) = p i ⋅ p j ⋅ ( 1 − p i ) ⋅ ( 1 − p j ) h(p_{i},p_{j})=\sqrt{p_{i}\cdot p_{j}\cdot(1-p_{i})\cdot(1-p_{j})} is the geometric mean of the variance terms. The correction factor is small when all ω i ​ j \omega_{ij} are small, meaning the combined probability approaches the independent product ∏ p i \prod p_{i} . Implication for CivicShield. Because CivicShield’s seven layers are drawn from five distinct fields (network security, formal methods, computational biology, aviation safety, cryptography), the pairwise feature overlaps ω i ​ j \omega_{ij} between cross-domain layers are structurally low. This provides a principled justification—beyond intuition—for why the cross-domain composition achieves better security than composing multiple defenses from the same domain (e.g., stacking multiple input filters). The composition theorem transforms CivicShield’s architectural philosophy from a design heuristic into a formally grounded advantage. TABLE VI: Sensitivity of Combined ASR to Layer Correlation Correlation ( ρ \rho ) Combined ASR Interpretation 0.0 (independent) 0.045% Idealized best case 0.3 (low correlation) 0.8% Optimistic realistic 0.5 (moderate) 3.5% Conservative realistic 0.7 (high correlation) 8.2% Pessimistic realistic Even under pessimistic correlation assumptions ( ρ = 0.7 \rho=0.7 ), the combined ASR of approximately 8% represents a substantial improvement over single-layer defenses ( > > 90% ASR)—roughly an order-of-magnitude reduction. Against unsophisticated attackers, the improvement is likely closer to two orders of magnitude. We emphasize that these estimates require empirical validation, which is the critical next step for this research. Caveat : The correlation factor ρ \rho is itself an estimate. Layers 3, 4, and 5 share dependence on semantic understanding of natural language, creating correlated failure modes. An attack that successfully mimics legitimate conversation semantics may evade all three layers simultaneously. Layer 6 (multi-model consensus) faces common-mode vulnerability when models share training data distributions. Empirical measurement of inter-layer failure correlation through the ablation methodology proposed in Section VII is essential to validate these estimates. VI Government Compliance Mapping A critical differentiator of CivicShield is its explicit design for government deployment compliance. This section maps the framework to applicable federal standards, regulations, and executive orders.

sections.heading: A-C Tightened Bound for Proposition 3 (Diversity-Correlation)
sections.text: Proposition 3. For defenses D i D_{i} , D j D_{j} with feature overlap ω ⁡ ( D i , D j ) \omega(D_{i},D_{j}) , the failure correlation satisfies ρ ⁡ ( f ​ a ​ i ​ l i , f ​ a ​ i ​ l j ) ≤ ω ⁡ ( D i , D j ) + ϵ \rho(fail_{i},fail_{j})\leq\omega(D_{i},D_{j})+\epsilon . We provide a tightened characterization of the residual term ϵ \epsilon . Proof. The failure correlation between two defenses can be decomposed into two components: Feature-dependent correlation. When both defenses process the same features of the input, a single adversarial perturbation can affect both simultaneously. The mutual information M ​ I ​ ( ϕ i ​ ( X ) , ϕ j ​ ( X ) ) MI(\phi_{i}(X);\phi_{j}(X)) quantifies the shared information, and the normalized overlap ω \omega bounds the fraction of the detection decision that is correlated. Formally, by the data processing inequality, the correlation between binary detection outcomes f ​ a ​ i ​ l i , f ​ a ​ i ​ l j fail_{i},fail_{j} is bounded by the correlation between the feature representations: ρ ⁡ ( f ​ a ​ i ​ l i , f ​ a ​ i ​ l j ) ≤ ρ ⁡ ( ϕ i ​ ( X ) , ϕ j ​ ( X ) ) ≤ ω ⁡ ( D i , D j ) \rho(fail_{i},fail_{j})\leq\rho(\phi_{i}(X),\phi_{j}(X))\leq\sqrt{\omega(D_{i},D_{j})} where the second inequality follows from the relationship between mutual information and Pearson correlation for jointly Gaussian variables (Equation 9.7.1 in Cover & Thomas). For non-Gaussian features, ω \omega provides an upper bound via the maximal correlation coefficient. Feature-independent correlation ( ϵ \epsilon ). The term ϵ \epsilon captures attacks that succeed regardless of the feature representation—i.e., attacks that are “universally evasive.” We define ϵ \epsilon formally as: ϵ = Pr ⁡ [ attack succeeds against ​ D i ​ AND ​ D j ∣ ϕ i ​ ( X ) ⟂ ϕ j ​ ( X ) ] \epsilon=\Pr[\text{attack succeeds against }D_{i}\text{ AND }D_{j}\mid\phi_{i}(X)\perp\phi_{j}(X)] This is the probability of simultaneous bypass even when the defenses use completely independent features. Following the beta-factor model from reliability engineering (IEC 61508), ϵ \epsilon can be estimated as: ϵ ≤ β C ​ C ​ F ⋅ min ⁡ ( p i , p j ) \epsilon\leq\beta_{CCF}\cdot\min(p_{i},p_{j}) where β C ​ C ​ F \beta_{CCF} is the common cause failure fraction and p i , p j p_{i},p_{j} are the individual bypass probabilities. For CivicShield’s cross-domain layers, β C ​ C ​ F \beta_{CCF} is bounded by the fraction of the attack taxonomy that is agnostic to detection mechanism. From our taxonomy (Table IV), only “universal bypass” attacks (e.g., Policy Puppetry exploiting training data artifacts) are feature-agnostic, representing approximately 1 of 8 attack families. We therefore estimate β C ​ C ​ F ≤ 0.15 \beta_{CCF}\leq 0.15 for cross-domain layer pairs, yielding ϵ ≤ 0.15 ⋅ min ⁡ ( p i , p j ) \epsilon\leq 0.15\cdot\min(p_{i},p_{j}) . Combined bound. Substituting: ρ ⁡ ( f ​ a ​ i ​ l i , f ​ a ​ i ​ l j ) ≤ ω ⁡ ( D i , D j ) + 0.15 ⋅ min ⁡ ( p i , p j ) \rho(fail_{i},fail_{j})\leq\sqrt{\omega(D_{i},D_{j})}+0.15\cdot\min(p_{i},p_{j}) For cross-domain pairs (e.g., L2 regex vs. L5 anomaly detection), ω ≈ 0.05 \omega\approx 0.05 – 0.15 0.15 , giving ρ ≤ 0.22 \rho\leq 0.22 – 0.39 + ϵ 0.39+\epsilon . For same-domain pairs (e.g., two regex-based filters), ω ≈ 0.7 \omega\approx 0.7 – 0.9 0.9 , giving ρ ≤ 0.84 \rho\leq 0.84 – 0.95 + ϵ 0.95+\epsilon . This quantitatively confirms the architectural advantage of cross-domain composition. ∎ Experimental support, please view the build logs for errors. Generated by L A T E xml .
